solution.concept_anchor: Speaker election vs removal — simple vs effective majority

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected by a simple majority of members of Lok Sabha present and voting, without any requirement for a minimum number of members to participate.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 93 uses the phrase 'chosen by the House' — this means an ordinary simple majority of members present and voting (provided quorum is met). There is no prescribed special majority or minimum participation beyond the quorum requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: The resolution for removal of the Speaker of Lok Sabha must be passed by a special majority — that is, two-thirds of the total membership of the House — before it can take effect.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 94 requires the removal resolution to be passed by 'a majority of all the then members of the House of the People' — this is effective majority, not a two-thirds special majority. Two-thirds majority is required under Article 368 for constitutional amendments, not for Speaker removal.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both election by simple majority and removal by 'high majority' may accept both as correct without verifying the specific type of majority for removal.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 93 — Speaker elected by simple majority (members present and voting). This is correct and unambiguous.

Evaluate Statement 2: Article 94 — removal by 'majority of all the then members' = effective majority, not two-thirds special majority. The statement incorrectly characterises this as a 'special majority of two-thirds'. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the phrase 'two-thirds of total membership' — a majority type students associate with high-stakes constitutional decisions. The removal of Speaker does require a higher threshold than ordinary business (effective majority vs simple majority), which makes a 'two-thirds' formulation feel plausible. However, Article 94 specifies 'majority of all the then members' — effective majority — not a two-thirds fraction. Conflating effective majority with special majority is the precise trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The contrast between election and removal of the Speaker is a key distinction in parliamentary law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Speaker is elected under Article 93 by the House — meaning by simple majority of members present and voting. Quorum (1/10th of total membership) must be present, but beyond that, whoever the majority of voters favour becomes Speaker.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 94 specifies removal by 'a majority of all the then members of the House of the People' — this is effective majority (calculated on current membership, excluding vacancies), not a two-thirds special majority. Two-thirds majority is a different constitutional threshold used, for example, under Article 368 for constitutional amendments and Article 249 for Rajya Sabha's special resolutions on State List.

Answer: (c) — Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The 14-day notice requirement before a removal resolution ensures transparency and allows preparation.
• Effective majority ≠ absolute majority ≠ special majority — these are three distinct thresholds.
• In practice, no Speaker of Lok Sabha has ever been removed through this process in India's parliamentary history.

solution.concept_anchor: PV Narasimha Rao case — bribery not covered by privilege
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. In PV Narasimha Rao v. State (1998), the SC held that an MP who accepted a bribe to vote a certain way on the floor of the House could not claim parliamentary privilege for the vote itself. The privilege covers the vote but not the anterior act of bribery — however, the SC majority held such MPs could not be prosecuted for the vote under privilege. The assertion as stated — that privilege does NOT cover the criminal act of bribe-taking — is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Article 105(2) protects freedom of speech and voting rights in Parliament, but this protection operates only within Parliament's precincts; it does not shield anterior criminal acts done outside the House.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The reason Parliament's privilege does not protect bribe-taking is precisely that Article 105(2) covers only what happens inside the House (the vote/speech) — the act of accepting a bribe occurs outside Parliament and is an independent criminal transaction. R directly explains A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a genuine (a) answer — both A and R are correct and R does explain A. The trap targets students who, having seen many (b) answers in assertion-reason questions where the causal link fails, instinctively doubt the causal connection here. However, R (territorial/scope limitation of Article 105) genuinely and directly explains A (why bribe-taking is not privileged) — the bribe is taken outside Parliament and Article 105 does not extend there. Students who mechanically apply 'probably (b)' without testing the causal link will miss this.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary privilege under Article 105 is one of the most nuanced areas of constitutional law.

Assertion (A): Correct. The Supreme Court's majority in PV Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) held that members who took bribes to vote in a particular way could not claim immunity under Article 105(2) for the act of bribery itself. The bribe-taking is a criminal act independent of and anterior to the parliamentary vote.

Reason (R): Correct. Article 105(2) protects members from court proceedings for 'anything said or any vote given' in Parliament. The crucial limitation is that this immunity is confined to acts done inside Parliament — the speech delivered, the vote cast. A bribe is solicited and received outside Parliament's precincts and thus falls outside the territorial and functional scope of Article 105.

Causal link: R directly explains A. It is precisely because Article 105's protection is limited to acts within Parliament that the prior criminal act of bribery outside the House is unprotected. R is the correct explanation of A.

Answer: (a)

Value Addition:
• The PV Narasimha Rao case (1998) involved the JMM bribery scandal during the 1993 confidence vote.
• Five-judge bench split: majority held that MPs who voted per bribe had immunity; those who took bribe but voted against had no immunity.
• Article 122 protects parliamentary proceedings from court scrutiny for procedural irregularities — a related but distinct privilege.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 329 — judicial bar on delimitation challenge
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may think the Delimitation Commission's non-statutory character makes it odd, without realising it is statutory — and therefore select the wrong option.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: Identify which three items share the attribute of being barred from judicial review/challenge under the Constitution.
Option (a) — Delimitation Commission orders: Article 329 bars courts from challenging delimitation orders. Falls in the 'judicially non-reviewable' category.
Option (b) — Speaker's Money Bill certificate: Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's certificate final — not subject to court challenge. Falls in same category.
Option (c) — Electoral rolls prepared by Election Commission: Article 329(b) bars challenging electoral rolls in courts except through election petition. Falls in same category.

Option (d) — Speaker's Tenth Schedule disqualification decision: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) specifically made this SUBJECT TO judicial review by striking down paragraph 7. This is the odd one out — it is reviewable, unlike the others.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: All four options involve the Election Commission/Speaker/Delimitation Commission acting in quasi-judicial or authoritative roles. The conflation trap merges two distinct categories: decisions that are final under the Constitution (options a, b, c) and decisions that appear final but are actually subject to judicial review (option d). A student who knows the broad principle 'electoral matters are not justiciable' will apply it uniformly and miss the Kihoto Hollohan exception for Tenth Schedule decisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution erects specific bars against judicial review in electoral and parliamentary matters, but these bars are not universal.

• Option (a): Delimitation Commission orders — Article 329(a) expressly bars any court from questioning the validity of any law relating to delimitation. Not reviewable. Belongs to the non-reviewable category.
• Option (b): Speaker's Money Bill certificate — Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's certificate final. Courts cannot question it. Belongs to non-reviewable category.
• Option (c): Electoral rolls prepared by the Election Commission — Article 329(b) bars courts from questioning electoral rolls except through election petitions. Belongs to the non-reviewable category.
• Option (d): Speaker's Tenth Schedule decision — this is the odd one out. While paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule originally barred judicial review, the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) struck down that paragraph and specifically held that the Speaker's disqualification decision IS subject to judicial review — though only after the final decision is made, not during proceedings.

Value Addition:
• Article 329 reflects the constitutional intent to keep electoral disputes out of ordinary courts — only election tribunals/petitions are the remedies.
• The Rojer Mathew case (2019) is testing whether the Money Bill certification bar (option b) should also be qualified — pending before a larger bench.
• Paragraph 6 of Tenth Schedule (saving provision for court bar on interim orders) was also affected by Kihoto Hollohan.

(c) The electoral rolls prepared by the Election Commission for conducting a general election to Lok Sabha

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker's functions — what belongs exclusively to Speaker

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over joint sittings of Parliament convened under Article 108.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 118(4) designates the Speaker of Lok Sabha as the presiding officer of joint sittings; the Vice-President does not preside.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and this certificate is final and cannot be challenged in any court.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 110(3) explicitly states that the Speaker's certificate on Money Bills is final.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha, when acting as adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule, can be overruled by the President of India if the President considers the proceedings to be biased.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule vests adjudicating power exclusively in the Speaker; the President has no role in Tenth Schedule proceedings. Only the courts (after final decision) can review the Speaker's Tenth Schedule decision.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is empowered to adjourn the House when quorum is absent, and no business can be transacted during such adjournment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100(3) requires the Speaker to adjourn or suspend a sitting when quorum is not present — no business can be transacted without quorum.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the Speaker's quasi-judicial role is subject to 'review' may substitute presidential oversight for judicial review, accepting Statement 3 and choosing (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 118(4) — Speaker presides at joint sittings. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 110(3) — Speaker's Money Bill certificate is final. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: President has NO role in Tenth Schedule proceedings — only Speaker decides, subject to court review. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4: Article 100(3) — Speaker adjourns when quorum absent. Correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the entity-swap trap — it replaces judicial review (courts reviewing the Speaker's Tenth Schedule decision) with presidential override. Students who know the Speaker's Tenth Schedule decision is reviewable may not recall that it is the courts (not the President) that review it. The President has absolutely no constitutional role in Tenth Schedule adjudication. Kihoto Hollohan established judicial (court) review — not executive (Presidential) override.
solution.final_explanation:
The Speaker of Lok Sabha exercises several constitutionally defined powers, each with its own reviewability status.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 118(4) designates the Speaker as the presiding officer of joint sittings under Article 108. The Vice-President of India (Rajya Sabha Chairman) has no presiding role at joint sittings.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 110(3) — the Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is constitutionally final and courts cannot question it (Article 329 read with Article 110).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The President has no role whatsoever in Tenth Schedule proceedings. The Speaker adjudicates disqualification, and only courts (after the final decision) can review the outcome. Kihoto Hollohan (1992) established this — it was the Supreme Court, not the President, that was given review jurisdiction.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 100(3) mandates the Speaker to adjourn or suspend the sitting when quorum is not met. No legislative business may be conducted in the absence of quorum.

Value Addition:
• The three joint sittings in India's history were all presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker.
• The quorum for Lok Sabha is 55 members (1/10th of 543); failure to maintain quorum is surprisingly common during routine sittings.
• The Speaker's salary and allowances are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India — ensuring independence from government control.

solution.concept_anchor: No-confidence motion — admission requirement of 50 members
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who confuse the admission threshold (50 members to support admission) with the passing threshold may think a higher number like 100 is required.
elimination_logic: Recall the procedural rule: A no-confidence motion in Lok Sabha requires the support of at least 50 members to be admitted by the Speaker.
Eliminate (a): No constitutional or statutory provision requires 100 members for admission of a no-confidence motion.
Eliminate (c): 1/10th of Lok Sabha strength ≈ 54 members relates to quorum, not the admission threshold for no-confidence motions.
Eliminate (d): 2/3rd of members is the special majority for constitutional amendments — not relevant to no-confidence motion admission.
Confirm (b): 50 members' support is the prescribed threshold for admission of a no-confidence motion.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) uses 1/10th of Lok Sabha strength (approximately 54 members), which is close to 50 and relates to quorum — a procedural number students know well. The proximity of 54 (quorum) and 50 (no-confidence admission) creates confusion. Students may dismiss 50 as 'too round a number' and prefer the 1/10th quorum fraction, choosing (c). In fact, Rule 198 of Lok Sabha Rules prescribes exactly 50 members' support — not a fractional calculation.
solution.final_explanation:
The no-confidence motion procedure in Lok Sabha is governed by Rule 198 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

• Option (a): Incorrect — 100 members is not prescribed anywhere as the support threshold for admitting a no-confidence motion.
• Option (b): Correct — Rule 198 requires that a no-confidence motion shall not be admitted unless it is supported by at least 50 members of the House when it is moved.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 1/10th of Lok Sabha membership (approximately 54) is the quorum requirement under Article 100(3), not the no-confidence motion admission threshold.
• Option (d): Incorrect — 2/3rd of members is a special majority threshold used in constitutional amendments and certain other provisions — not applicable to no-confidence motion admission.

Value Addition:
• Once admitted, the Speaker allots a date for debate on the motion within 10 days.
• If the motion is passed, the Council of Ministers is bound to resign collectively.
• The most recent successful no-confidence motion was in 1999 against the Vajpayee government, which lost by one vote.
• Confidence motions (moved by the government itself) require simple majority to pass — same as no-confidence.

(d) Two-thirds of the members present and voting on the day the motion is moved

solution.concept_anchor: Delimitation freeze — 42nd vs 84th Amendment sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may place the 84th Amendment before the 42nd because they associate 84th Amendment with 'more recent' delimitation changes, without knowing the chronology.
elimination_logic: Place Event 1: The Constitution came into force in 1950 — establishing the original provisions for delimitation after each Census.
Place Event 2: The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat allocation based on the 1971 Census — first freeze. Comes after 1950 and after the 1971 Census.
Place Event 3: The 84th Amendment (2001) was enacted after the 2001 Census to extend the freeze until after the first Census post-2026.
Place Event 4: The 104th Amendment (2019) abolished Anglo-Indian nomination — most recent.
Correct order: Original Constitution → 42nd Amendment (1976) → 84th Amendment (2001) → 104th Amendment (2019) = answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary temporal trap is swapping the 42nd and 84th Amendments. Both deal with seat/representation issues in Parliament but were enacted 25 years apart. The 42nd Amendment is associated with the Emergency period (1976) and froze delimitation. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended that freeze. A student who cannot place these amendments chronologically may reverse them, choosing option (c) or (d).
solution.final_explanation:
Several constitutional amendments have successively shaped Lok Sabha's composition and delimitation framework.

Correct chronological order:
1. Original Constitution, 1950: Established provisions for delimitation after each Census without a freeze.
2. 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Emergency period): Froze readjustment of Lok Sabha seats based on 1971 Census figures — principally to prevent states that had implemented family planning from losing seats.
3. 84th Amendment, 2001: Extended the freeze on seat readjustment until after the first Census following 2026.
4. 104th Amendment, 2019: Abolished Anglo-Indian nominated seats in Lok Sabha (Article 331) and State Assemblies (Article 333) and extended SC/ST reservation to 2030.

Wrong options introduce errors by placing the 42nd Amendment after the 84th (impossible — lower amendment number = earlier) or by placing the 104th Amendment before the 84th.

Value Addition:
• The 2026 deadline means the next delimitation will be based on the 2031 Census (first Census after 2026).
• The 42nd Amendment was one of the most sweeping amendments — it also curtailed judicial review and expanded Parliament's power.
• The 84th Amendment also rationalised assembly constituencies using 1991 Census data.

Election of the Speaker of Lok Sabha

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker-elect resigning from party — special Tenth Schedule protection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the Tenth Schedule disqualifies members who voluntarily give up party membership may immediately apply this rule without recalling the special exception for the Speaker.
elimination_logic: Identify the governing rule: The Tenth Schedule provides that a member who voluntarily gives up party membership is disqualified. However, a special convention and legal understanding protects the Speaker — a member elected as Speaker may resign from their party without inviting Tenth Schedule disqualification, in order to maintain the office's neutrality.
Eliminate (a): Applying the standard Tenth Schedule rule without the Speaker exception leads to disqualification — but the Speaker has special protection. Incorrect.
Eliminate (b): Effective majority for removal is a separate process unrelated to Tenth Schedule disqualification. Incorrect.
Eliminate (c): The President has no role in Tenth Schedule proceedings. Incorrect.

Confirm (d): The special protection for the Speaker under the Tenth Schedule means that resignation from the party upon assuming the Speakership does not attract disqualification. This preserves the office's constitutional neutrality.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario perfectly mimics a standard Tenth Schedule disqualification case — voluntary resignation from party. A student who applies the general anti-defection rule will choose (a) without recalling the specific exception for the Speaker. The Tenth Schedule itself and related constitutional conventions recognise that requiring the Speaker to maintain party membership would compromise the constitutional neutrality of the office. This is a scope-extension trap — extending the anti-defection rule to a context (Speaker's office) where it is specifically carved out.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule creates a specific exemption for the Speaker of Lok Sabha — one that reflects a fundamental constitutional principle: the neutrality of the presiding officer.

Applicable principle: A member who voluntarily resigns from their party after being elected as Speaker does not attract Tenth Schedule disqualification. This exception is grounded in the constitutional understanding that the Speaker must be neutral and impartial, which is inconsistent with maintaining active party membership. This protection is recognised in the constitutional scheme, even though the Tenth Schedule's text focuses on merger exceptions.

• Option (a): Incorrect — mechanically applying Tenth Schedule ignores the Speaker's special constitutional position. The disqualification does not apply.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the effective majority removal process under Article 94 is an entirely different mechanism requiring a formal resolution and 14 days' notice. Resignation from party does not trigger it.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the President acts on the Election Commission's opinion for Article 102 disqualifications. Tenth Schedule matters go to the Speaker (or, in this scenario, since the Speaker himself is involved, the Deputy Speaker or a mechanism determined by the House).
• Option (d): Correct — the Speaker is constitutionally protected from Tenth Schedule disqualification for resigning from their party after election to the Speakership.

Value Addition:
• UK's House of Commons Speaker traditionally resigns from the party immediately on election.
• India's constitutional convention similarly expects the Speaker to be above party politics.
• The Tenth Schedule's merger exception requires 2/3rd of legislative party members — completely separate from the Speaker protection.

solution.concept_anchor: Quorum vs majority — distinct thresholds, both Houses same quorum

statement_analysis.statement: The quorum for Lok Sabha (1/10th of total membership) is a lower fraction than the quorum prescribed for Rajya Sabha, reflecting the larger size of the lower house.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100(3) prescribes 1/10th of total membership as quorum for BOTH Houses — the fraction is identical regardless of the size difference between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

statement_analysis.statement: A constitutional amendment under Article 368 requires, among other conditions, that 2/3rd of the total membership of each House must vote in favour — the votes of absent members count as abstentions.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 requires 2/3rd of members PRESENT AND VOTING (not total membership) plus majority of total membership. Absent members are not factored as abstentions — only those present and voting are counted in the 2/3rd calculation.

statement_analysis.statement: In the event of equality of votes on a motion in Lok Sabha, the Speaker exercises a casting vote, and this casting vote is given the same weight as the vote of any other member.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100(1) provides that the Speaker exercises a casting vote in case of equality, and constitutionally this casting vote resolves the deadlock — it is treated as determinative and equal in weight to any other vote.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Rajya Sabha is smaller may intuitively (but incorrectly) assume different quorum fractions, making Statement 1 feel possibly correct and choosing (a) as the answer.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Article 100(3) uses the same 1/10th fraction for both Houses — the fraction does not vary by House size. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Test Statement 2: Article 368 says '2/3rd of members present and voting' NOT 2/3rd of total membership. Absent members are not counted as abstentions. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Test Statement 3: The casting vote under Article 100(1) does carry equal weight and resolves the tie — this is correct.
Two statements (1 and 2) are NOT correct — answer is (c) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses an authoritative-sounding formulation — '2/3rd of total membership' with 'absent members counted as abstentions'. This is a conflation of two different majority types: the 2/3rd fraction is correct, but it applies to 'present and voting', not 'total membership'. Additionally, absent members are simply absent — the Constitution does not deem them abstaining. Students who have memorised '2/3rd' without retaining 'present and voting' will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between quorum and different types of majority is one of the most precise areas tested in UPSC Polity.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 100(3) prescribes 1/10th of total membership as quorum for both Houses of Parliament. The larger size of Lok Sabha means a larger absolute number is required (approximately 55 vs approximately 25 for Rajya Sabha), but the fraction is identical — 1/10th in both cases.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 368(2) requires that the amendment be passed in each House 'by a majority of the total membership of that House AND by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting'. The 2/3rd fraction is of members present and voting — not of total membership. Absent members are simply absent; they are not counted as abstentions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Speaker's casting vote under Article 100(1) is exercised when votes are equal. It carries full weight and is not different from any other member's vote in legal effect — it resolves the deadlock with finality.

Value Addition:
• Some constitutional amendments additionally require ratification by at least half the state legislatures — adding a third layer beyond both 2/3rd conditions.
• The same Article 368 voting formula applies to both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — both Houses must independently satisfy the threshold.
• A member who is present but abstains counts as 'present and voting' for quorum but NOT in the 2/3rd calculation.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 110 — 7 Money Bill matters, Rajya Sabha's 14-day limit
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the Aadhaar Act was challenged as a Money Bill may think the challenge was successful, incorrectly selecting (c) as correctly matched.
elimination_logic: Option (a): States Article 110 lists 5 matters — incorrect, Article 110(1) lists 7 specific matters that define a Money Bill.
Option (b): States Rajya Sabha's role on a Money Bill is limited to 14-day recommendations that are not binding on Lok Sabha — this is correct under Articles 109 and 110.

Option (c): States the Supreme Court in Rojer Mathew case struck down the Aadhaar Act's Money Bill certification — incorrect. The SC referred the matter to a larger bench but did not strike down the certification.

Option (d): States Finance Bills are always treated as Money Bills — incorrect. Finance Bills that contain non-Money Bill provisions are not certified as Money Bills and Rajya Sabha retains full powers.
Confirm (b) as correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) exploits the widely-known Aadhaar Act controversy. Students who followed the Rojer Mathew case may recall that the Supreme Court questioned the Money Bill certification but cannot recall the precise outcome — the case was referred to a larger bench, not decided. Stating that the SC 'struck down' the certification is a temporal fabrication — the case was pending before a larger bench as of the last known proceedings. This is a conflation of 'referred for reconsideration' with 'struck down'.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 110 defines Money Bills and establishes the Speaker's certification role.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched — Article 110(1) lists seven specific categories, not five. These cover taxation, borrowing, Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, appropriation, audit, and related matters.
• Option (b): Correctly matched — Articles 109 and 110 together limit Rajya Sabha's role on a Money Bill to making recommendations within 14 days, which Lok Sabha may accept or reject. Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched — In Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2019), a five-judge bench referred the question of the Aadhaar Act's Money Bill certification to a larger seven-judge bench. The certification was not struck down; the larger bench hearing is pending.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — A Finance Bill is not automatically a Money Bill. The Finance Bill accompanying the Union Budget often contains provisions beyond the seven Article 110 matters. For those additional provisions, Rajya Sabha retains full legislative power.

Value Addition:
• If Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed in the form sent by Lok Sabha.
• Rajya Sabha cannot withhold a Money Bill — only recommend changes.
• The definition of Money Bill under Article 110 is exhaustive — any bill that deals with even one non-Money Bill matter cannot be certified as a Money Bill.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker vacation — before first sitting of new House, not at dissolution

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of Lok Sabha vacates office immediately upon dissolution of Lok Sabha, since dissolution terminates all offices that derive from the House's existence.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 94(c) provides that the Speaker vacates office immediately before the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha after a general election — NOT at the time of dissolution. The Speaker continues in office even after dissolution until the new House first meets.

statement_analysis.statement: The procedure for removing the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha is identical to that for removing the Speaker — requiring an effective majority and 14 days' prior notice.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 94 covers both Speaker and Deputy Speaker removal under the same provision — effective majority (majority of all then members) and 14 days' notice apply to both.

statement_analysis.statement: During the period between dissolution of Lok Sabha and the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha, the Speaker continues to hold office but cannot exercise the powers of the Speakership as there is no House in session.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Speaker's role is naturally limited during dissolution (no House to preside over), the Speaker technically continues to hold the constitutional office. However, saying the Speaker 'cannot exercise any powers' is overstated — the Speaker retains administrative powers related to Parliament's secretariat and, critically, continues to hold the office.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the Speaker continues after dissolution but overapply this to say all three statements about continuity are correct may choose (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 94(c) — Speaker vacates before first sitting of new House, NOT at dissolution. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 94 explicitly covers Deputy Speaker under the same removal procedure. Statement 2 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: The Speaker continues in office after dissolution — the claim that the Speaker 'cannot exercise the powers of the Speakership' is partially true (no House to preside) but overstated as a blanket assertion. Administrative powers remain. More precisely, Statement 3 correctly notes no House is in session, but 'cannot exercise any powers' is too sweeping. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is correct — answer is (b) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the natural but incorrect assumption that dissolution ends all offices tied to the House. Article 94(c) is precise: the Speaker continues even after dissolution. This is a deliberate design to avoid a vacuum — there must be a Speaker to convene the new House. Statement 3 compounds the confusion by adding a plausible-sounding qualification about the dissolved House, leading students who partially know Statement 1 is wrong to nonetheless doubt Statement 3's precise characterisation.
solution.final_explanation:
The tenure of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker post-dissolution is one of the most precisely drafted constitutional provisions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The critical constitutional provision is Article 94(c): the Speaker vacates office 'immediately before the first sitting of the House of the People after its dissolution'. This means the Speaker continues in office throughout the dissolution period — potentially weeks or months — until the new Lok Sabha convenes for its very first sitting. This prevents a constitutional vacuum.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 94 covers both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker in a single provision. Both require a resolution passed by effective majority (majority of all then members) and both require 14 days' advance notice before such a resolution can be moved.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: While the Speaker has no House to preside over during dissolution (no sessions can be held), characterising this as inability to 'exercise powers' is imprecise. The Speaker retains the constitutional office and exercises administrative powers over the Secretariat. The statement is substantively misleading.

Value Addition:
• The Pro-tem Speaker's appointment by the President effectively coincides with the outgoing Speaker vacating office.
• No Deputy Speaker has been appointed in recent Lok Sabhas — the 17th Lok Sabha (2019–2024) did not have a Deputy Speaker.
• The constitutional continuity of the Speaker post-dissolution is a unique feature distinguishing Indian constitutional design from a strict Westminster model.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 84 — minimum age 25 for Lok Sabha membership
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who confuse the minimum age for Lok Sabha (25) with the minimum age for Rajya Sabha (30) may choose (b) if they apply the wrong House's qualification.
elimination_logic: Recall Article 84(b): A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in the House of the People unless they are not less than 25 years of age.
Eliminate (b): 30 years is the minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership, not Lok Sabha.
Eliminate (c): 21 years is the voting age (right to vote), not the candidacy age.
Eliminate (d): 35 years is the minimum age for the office of President of India.
Confirm (a): 25 years is the correct minimum age for Lok Sabha membership under Article 84.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the temporal-swap distractor, substituting Rajya Sabha's age qualification (30 years) for Lok Sabha's (25 years). This is a classic entity-swap where the correct age is paired with the wrong House. Students who have memorised ages without firmly anchoring them to the correct House will choose (b). The three ages — 25 (Lok Sabha), 30 (Rajya Sabha), 35 (President) — are a perennial source of confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 84 prescribes qualifications for membership of Parliament.

• Option (a): Correct — Article 84(b) requires a person to be not less than 25 years of age to be elected to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
• Option (b): Incorrect — 30 years is the minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership under Article 84(b). Applying this to Lok Sabha is an entity-swap error.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 21 years was the former voting age, now 18 years. Neither is the minimum candidacy age for Lok Sabha.
• Option (d): Incorrect — 35 years is the minimum age prescribed under Article 58 for election as President of India.

Value Addition:
• Minimum age for election as Vice-President: 35 years (Article 66).
• Minimum age for election as Governor: 35 years (Article 157).
• Minimum age for election to State Legislative Assembly: 25 years (Article 173) — same as Lok Sabha.
• Minimum age for State Legislative Council: 30 years — same as Rajya Sabha.
